azapi_resource.diag_settings publishes diagnostic settings whose workspaceId is derived only from a plain string (local.template_file_variables.log_analytics_workspace_resource_id), so Terraform has no ordering edge to azurerm_log_analytics_workspace.management. When deploy_management_resources is true this module creates that workspace; without a dependency the diagnostic settings (and the DDOS/diag policies) can be applied before the destination Log Analytics workspace exists. Add a dependency (e.g. depends_on) on azurerm_log_analytics_workspace.management.

----------------------------------------

[final-deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-effort-high-run2]
azapi_resource.diag_settings sends its diagnostic logs to `workspaceId = local.template_file_variables.log_analytics_workspace_resource_id`, which is only a string derived from module outputs (no resource reference is created). Its depends_on only covers the Management Group hierarchy and time_sleep.after_azurerm_management_group, so the subscription/tenant-level diagnostic setting can be created before azurerm_log_analytics_workspace.management exists and the Azure API call will fail. It must be ordered after the Log Analytics workspace (which in turn follows azurerm_resource_group.management).

Nothing orders it after the workspace, so the diagnostic setting can be applied before the workspace exists and fail with a not-found workspace.

When an attachment references a policy created by this module, the apply may fail because the policy does not yet exist. The association should depend on google_compute_organization_security_policy.policy (e.g. explicit depends_on), since no clean data reference is available (attachment keys don't correspond to the policy map keys).

Because there is no attribute reference or `depends_on` between them, Terraform can create/associate the policy before the policy exists on a first apply (the provider's own example sets `policy_id = google_compute_organization_security_policy.policy.id`). The association should be ordered after the security policy — e.g. `policy_id = try(google_compute_organization_security_policy.policy[each.key].id, each.value)` so a module-created policy is referenced when the attachment key matches a policy key and externally supplied IDs still win otherwise, or a bare `depends_on = [google_compute_organization_security_policy.policy]`.

`google_project_iam_member.additive` grants whatever roles are listed in `var.iam_additive_roles`, which can include the custom roles created by `google_project_iam_custom_role.roles` in this same module. A role cannot be granted before it exists, so the additive member must be ordered after the custom role. The sibling authoritative binding already expresses exactly this ordering with `depends_on = [google_project_iam_custom_role.roles]`, but the additive member relies only on input variables, so no implicit dependency exists and the two can race.

The authoritative counterpart `google_project_iam_binding.authoritative` explicitly orders itself after `google_project_iam_custom_role.roles` for exactly this reason; the additive members should do the same via `depends_on = [google_project_iam_custom_role.roles]`.

This is the same ordering the module already encodes for `google_compute_project_metadata_item.oslogin_meta` ("depend on services or it will fail on destroy"). The spoke references the appliance VMs only through `var.router_appliances`, so it has no dependency on `peer_0` and Terraform may create the spoke before the BGP peering exists. Order the spoke after `google_compute_router_peer.peer_0` (e.g. via `depends_on`).

NCC requires the BGP sessions between the Cloud Router interfaces and the router appliance VMs to be established before the router appliance spoke can be created, so peer_0 must be created (and its session up) first; otherwise the spoke create can fail or be flaky. Add an explicit depends_on on google_compute_router_peer.peer_0 (and peer_1) since no spoke attribute can reference a router peer.
